module.title: Prepositions of Movement: Into, Out of & Across
module.objective: Describe routes and movement through spaces accurately using prepositions of motion (into, out of, across, through, along, past).

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Follow the Route!
subModules.theme: Prepositions of Movement in Everyday Journeys
subModules.grammarFocus: Prepositions of Movement: into, out of, across, through, along, past
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Places, routes, and movement words for giving and understanding directions

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you will read a fun story about a person's journey through a town. You will learn how to understand prepositions of movement — words like INTO, OUT OF, ACROSS, THROUGH, ALONG, and PAST. These small words tell us HOW someone moves from one place to another. By the end of this mission, you will be able to read simple directions and understand routes. Let's go on an adventure!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Prepositions of movement (into, out of, across, through, along, past) used with action verbs like walk, run, drive, and go to describe routes and directions.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Places in a town (bridge, tunnel, park, street, building, gate, corner, entrance, exit, path) and action verbs of movement.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for movement words: Look for prepositions of movement (into, out of, across, through, along, past) to understand the direction and route described in a passage. Visualize the journey like a map in your mind!

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about someone's journey through a town.
Identify key details about WHERE a person goes and HOW they move (into a building, across a bridge, etc.).
Recognize and distinguish the six prepositions of movement: into, out of, across, through, along, and past.
Use context clues to understand the meaning of movement sentences in a reading passage.

contextWarmup.prompt: Imagine you are walking to school. You walk ACROSS a bridge and then go INTO your school building. Which preposition describes moving from one side of the bridge to the other side?
options: across
into
out of
contextWarmup.explanation: Great job! 'Across' means moving from one side to the other side of something, like a bridge or a street. 'Into' means entering something, and 'out of' means leaving something.

rules: INTO means moving from outside to inside something. Example: 'She walked into the shop.' Picture an arrow going IN through a door.
OUT OF means moving from inside to outside something. It is the opposite of INTO. Example: 'He ran out of the house.' Picture an arrow coming OUT through a door.
ACROSS means moving from one side to the other side of a surface or open area. Example: 'They walked across the park.' Picture a line going from left to right over a flat space.
THROUGH means moving from one end to the other end INSIDE something. Example: 'The train went through the tunnel.' Picture going inside and coming out the other end.
ALONG means moving forward following a line, road, or path. Example: 'Walk along this street.' Picture following a road straight ahead.
PAST means moving beside something and continuing forward without stopping. Example: 'Go past the bank.' Picture passing a building on your left or right.

commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners confuse ACROSS and THROUGH. Remember: ACROSS is for flat, open surfaces (a bridge, a road, a field). THROUGH is for enclosed spaces where you go INSIDE (a tunnel, a forest, a gate). Also, do not confuse INTO (one word, meaning 'enter') with IN TO (two separate words). 'She walked into the room' means she entered the room. 'She walked in to say hello' means she walked in FOR THE PURPOSE of saying hello.
commonTrap.wrong: He drove across the tunnel. (A tunnel is enclosed — you go INSIDE it, not over its surface.)
commonTrap.correct: He drove through the tunnel. (THROUGH is correct because you enter one end and exit the other end.)

content.context: Maya lives in a small town. Every morning, she walks from her house to the library. Read about her route and notice the prepositions of movement!
content.text:
Every morning, Maya walks out of her house at 7 o'clock. She closes the gate and walks along the quiet street. There are many trees along the path. After five minutes, she goes past a small coffee shop on the corner. She does not stop there today.

Next, Maya walks across the old bridge over the river. She likes to look at the water. On the other side, she goes through the town park. Children are playing there, and birds are singing in the trees.

After the park, Maya walks past the post office and the market. Finally, she arrives at the library. She walks through the main entrance and into the reading room. She sits down, opens her book, and smiles. It is a beautiful morning for reading!

highlights.note: Preposition of movement: leaving the inside of a place (her house).
Preposition of movement: following the direction of a road or path.
Preposition of movement: moving beside something and continuing forward.
Preposition of movement: from one side to the other side of a surface (the bridge).
Preposition of movement: moving from one end to the other inside a space (the park, the entrance).
Preposition of movement: entering a space (the reading room).
A structure built over a river or road so people can cross.
The door or opening where you go into a building.
The point where two streets or walls meet.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is this passage mainly about?
options: Maya's walking route from her house to the library.
Maya's favourite food at the coffee shop.
Maya's friends in the town park.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage describes Maya's journey — her route from her house to the library. It tells us all the places she walks past, through, and across. The coffee shop and the park are just places on her route, not the main topic.

detailQuestions.prompt: What does Maya do first when she leaves her house?
options: She walks out of her house and along the quiet street.
She walks across the bridge over the river.
She goes into the coffee shop on the corner.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'Maya walks out of her house at 7 o'clock. She closes the gate and walks along the quiet street.' This is the first thing she does. The bridge and coffee shop come later in her route.

detailQuestions.prompt: How does Maya cross the river?
options: She walks across the old bridge.
She swims through the river.
She drives past the river.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'Maya walks across the old bridge over the river.' The word 'across' tells us she goes from one side of the bridge to the other side. She does not swim or drive.

detailQuestions.prompt: Where does Maya go after walking through the town park?
options: She walks past the post office and the market.
She walks back to her house.
She goes into the coffee shop.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'After the park, Maya walks past the post office and the market.' The word 'past' means she goes beside these places and continues walking without stopping.

detailQuestions.prompt: How does Maya enter the library?
options: She walks through the main entrance and into the reading room.
She runs across the library and out of the exit.
She goes past the library and along the street.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'She walks through the main entrance and into the reading room.' 'Through' means she passes from one side of the entrance to the other, and 'into' means she enters the reading room.

questions.question: In the passage, Maya 'walks out of her house.' What does 'out of' mean here?
options: Leaving the inside of a place.
Entering a place.
Walking beside a place.
questions.answer: Leaving the inside of a place.
questions.explanation: 'Out of' is a preposition of movement that means leaving the inside of something. Maya was inside her house, and she moved to the outside. It is the opposite of 'into.'

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses the preposition 'across' correctly?
options: Maya walks across the old bridge over the river.
Maya walks across her house at 7 o'clock.
Maya walks across the main entrance.
questions.answer: Maya walks across the old bridge over the river.
questions.explanation: 'Across' means moving from one side to the other side of a flat surface or structure. A bridge is something you cross from one side to the other. You do not walk 'across' a house or an entrance — you walk 'out of' a house and 'through' an entrance.

questions.question: Read this sentence: 'She goes through the town park.' What does 'through' tell us?
options: Maya moves from one end of the park to the other end, passing inside it.
Maya stops and stays inside the park.
Maya walks beside the park without entering it.
questions.answer: Maya moves from one end of the park to the other end, passing inside it.
questions.explanation: 'Through' means moving from one end to the other end of a space, passing inside it. Maya enters the park on one side and comes out on the other side. She does not stop there or walk beside it.

questions.question: Maya 'walks past the coffee shop.' Does she go inside the coffee shop?
options: No, she walks beside it and continues forward without stopping.
Yes, she goes into the coffee shop to buy coffee.
Yes, she walks through the coffee shop.
questions.answer: No, she walks beside it and continues forward without stopping.
questions.explanation: 'Past' means moving beside something and continuing forward. The passage also says 'She does not stop there today.' So Maya does not enter the coffee shop — she just passes it.

questions.question: Choose the correct preposition: 'The children ran _____ the gate and _____ the playground.' (They entered through the gate and then entered the playground.)
options: through / into
past / out of
along / across
questions.explanation: 'Through the gate' means passing from one side of the gate to the other. 'Into the playground' means entering the playground. Together, these prepositions describe the children's movement: they passed through the gate and entered the playground.

questions.question: Which preposition completes this sentence correctly? 'He walked _____ the long street to get to the shop.'
options: along
into
out of
questions.explanation: 'Along' means following the direction of a road, street, or path. 'He walked along the long street' means he followed the street from one point to another. 'Into' means entering, and 'out of' means leaving — neither fits here.

questions.question: Look at the passage again. Put Maya's route in the correct order. Which comes FIRST?
options: She walks along the quiet street.
She walks across the old bridge.
She goes through the town park.
questions.answer: She walks along the quiet street.
questions.explanation: According to the passage, Maya first walks out of her house and then walks along the quiet street. After that, she goes past the coffee shop, then across the bridge, and then through the park. So walking along the street comes first.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Finding the Way to the City Library

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a conversation between Sarah and a local person on the street. Sarah asks for directions to the city library. The local person explains the route using prepositions of movement such as 'into', 'out of', 'across', 'through', 'along', and 'past'. Listen carefully for these prepositions because they tell you the direction and path of movement. Pay attention to the order of the steps in the directions. When people give directions in English, they often use short, clear sentences with one or two prepositions of movement in each sentence.
learningObjectives: Identify prepositions of movement (into, out of, across, through, along, past) when heard in natural spoken English.
Understand a sequence of directions given in a real-life conversation about finding a place.
Distinguish between different prepositions of movement based on the type of movement described (e.g., crossing something vs. going inside something).
Follow a multi-step route described using prepositions of movement in spoken English.

keyPhrases.note: Use 'along' when you follow the length of a road, river, or path without turning.
Use 'past' when you walk by something and leave it behind you. You do not stop there.
Use 'across' when you move from one side of something to the other side, like a bridge, a road, or a field.
Use 'through' when you enter one side of a place and come out the other side. You move inside the space.
Use 'out of' when you leave an enclosed or defined area. It is the opposite of 'into'.
Use 'into' when you move from outside to inside a place. It shows entering a space.

connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'walk' and 'along' link together because 'walk' ends with a consonant /k/ and 'along' starts with a vowel /ə/. It sounds like 'walkalong'.
In fast speech, the /t/ at the end of 'past' is often dropped or softened before the /ð/ sound in 'the'. It may sound like 'pas the'.
In natural speech, 'walk' and 'across' link together smoothly. The /k/ at the end of 'walk' connects to the /ə/ at the start of 'across'.
In fast speech, 'out' and 'of' blend together. The /t/ in 'out' links to the /ɒ/ in 'of', sounding like 'outov' or even 'outta' in very casual speech.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: Asking for Directions to the City Library

content.context: Sarah is visiting a new city. She is standing on a busy street and she needs to find the city library. She stops a friendly local person and asks for directions. The local person explains the route step by step using prepositions of movement.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between Sarah and a local person giving directions. Pay close attention to the prepositions of movement they use.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Excuse me, how do I get to the city library?
lines.translation: Permisi, bagaimana cara saya ke perpustakaan kota?

lines.speaker: Local
lines.text: Sure! Walk along this street for two blocks.
lines.translation: Tentu! Berjalan mengikuti jalan ini selama dua blok.

lines.speaker: Local
lines.text: Go past the coffee shop and turn right at the corner.
lines.translation: Lewati kedai kopi dan belok kanan di pojok.

lines.speaker: Local
lines.text: Walk across the bridge and through the park.
lines.translation: Berjalan melintasi jembatan dan melewati taman.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Is the library after the park?

lines.speaker: Local
lines.text: Yes! When you come out of the park, the library is right there.
lines.translation: Ya! Ketika Anda keluar dari taman, perpustakaan ada tepat di sana.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Great! So I go into the park from the bridge side?
lines.translation: Bagus! Jadi saya masuk ke taman dari sisi jembatan?

lines.speaker: Local
lines.text: Exactly! Walk through the park and out of the gate on the other side. You will see the library.
lines.translation: Tepat! Berjalan melewati taman dan keluar dari gerbang di sisi lain. Anda akan melihat perpustakaan.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Describe Routes with Prepositions of Movement

content.summary: In this lesson, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about movement and routes. You will use six prepositions of movement: INTO (entering something), OUT OF (leaving something), ACROSS (going from one side to the other side), THROUGH (going inside and coming out the other end), ALONG (following a road or path), and PAST (going by something without stopping). Each preposition follows a simple formula: Subject + Verb + Preposition + Place. Let us learn step by step how to build clear sentences about how people and things move from one place to another.

blueprintItems.title: Choose Your Subject and Movement Verb
blueprintItems.example: The cat ran / She walked / We drove / He cycled

blueprintItems.title: Add the Correct Preposition of Movement
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Verb + INTO / OUT OF / ACROSS / THROUGH / ALONG / PAST
blueprintItems.example: The cat ran into / She walked out of / We drove through / He cycled along

blueprintItems.title: Add the Place or Location
blueprintItems.example: The cat ran into the kitchen. She walked out of the shop. We drove through the tunnel.

blueprintItems.title: Connect Two or More Movements to Describe a Route
blueprintItems.example: I walked along the street and then I went across the bridge.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always start a sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.
mechanicsRules.why: Every English sentence must begin with a capital letter and finish with a full stop (period). This shows where the sentence starts and ends.

mechanicsRules.rule: OUT OF is always two words. Never write 'outof' as one word.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He ran out of the building.
mechanicsRules.why: OUT OF is a two-word preposition. You must always write a space between 'out' and 'of' to be correct.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'the' or 'a' before the place noun after the preposition.
mechanicsRules.why: In English, most place nouns need an article (the, a, an) before them. Without the article, the sentence sounds incomplete.

mechanicsRules.rule: Do not confuse THROUGH and ACROSS. THROUGH means going inside something (like a tunnel). ACROSS means going from one side to the other side of a flat surface (like a road).
mechanicsRules.why: A road is a flat surface, so you go ACROSS it. You go THROUGH things that surround you, like a tunnel, a forest, or a door.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (at least 4 sentences) about your journey from home to your favourite place. Use at least 4 different prepositions of movement (choose from: INTO, OUT OF, ACROSS, THROUGH, ALONG, PAST).

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Giving Directions with Movement Prepositions

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise saying directions using prepositions of movement: into, out of, across, through, along, and past. You will learn how to pronounce these prepositions clearly and use them in full sentences when telling someone how to get from one place to another. Good pronunciation and natural rhythm will help people understand your directions easily.
content.audioGuidance: Pay attention to how prepositions connect to the next word. For example, 'into the' sounds like /ˈɪn.tə ðə/, not three separate words. The word 'across' has stress on the second syllable: a-CROSS. 'Out of' is often reduced to /ˈaʊt.əv/ in natural speech. Practise linking words together smoothly, and use falling intonation at the end of direction sentences because they are instructions.

pillars.name: Preposition Clarity
pillars.target: Pronounce each movement preposition clearly and correctly
pillars.explanation: Each preposition of movement has its own pronunciation pattern. 'Into' is stressed on the first syllable: IN-to. 'Out of' links together as one unit. 'Across' is stressed on the second syllable: a-CROSS. 'Through' uses the /θruː/ sound. 'Along' is stressed on the second syllable: a-LONG. 'Past' rhymes with 'fast'. Practise each one separately before using them in sentences.

pillars.name: Sentence Rhythm
pillars.target: Use natural stress and rhythm when giving directions
pillars.explanation: When you give directions, the important words (verbs and place names) get more stress. For example: 'WALK aLONG Park STREET.' The small words like 'the' and 'a' are spoken quickly and softly. This creates a natural English rhythm that is easy to understand.

pillars.name: Intonation for Instructions
pillars.target: Use falling intonation for direction commands
pillars.explanation: Directions are usually imperative sentences (commands). In English, commands use falling intonation at the end. For example: 'Go INTO the building.' ↘ Your voice should go down at the end. This sounds confident and clear. If your voice goes up, it sounds like a question, which can confuse the listener.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The correct stress for 'into' is on the first syllable: IN-to. Some learners put stress on the second syllable by mistake. Always say IN-to with a strong first syllable.
The correct stress for 'across' is on the second syllable: a-CROSS. Do not stress the first syllable. The 'a' at the beginning is very short and weak, like /ə/.
The correct stress for 'along' is on the second syllable: a-LONG. The first 'a' is reduced to a short schwa sound /ə/. Make sure 'LONG' is the louder, longer syllable.

drills.hint: Say 'IN-to' as one smooth unit. Link it to 'the' so it sounds like 'IN-tuh-thuh'. Your voice should fall at the end.
Say 'out of' quickly together: 'OWT-uv'. Do not pause between 'out' and 'of'. The 'of' is reduced to /əv/.

drills.focus: Stress on the second syllable of 'across'
drills.hint: Remember: a-CROSS, not AC-ross. The 'a' is very short. Stress the 'CROSS' part clearly.
Put your tongue between your teeth for the /θ/ sound, then quickly move to the /r/. 'Through' rhymes with 'blue'.

drills.focus: Stress on the second syllable of 'along'
drills.hint: Say a-LONG with stress on 'LONG'. The first 'a' is very quick and soft.

drills.targetText: Go past the hospital and turn left.
drills.phonetic: /ɡəʊ pɑːst ðə ˈhɒs.pɪ.təl ənd tɜːn left/
drills.focus: Clear pronunciation of 'past' and sentence rhythm
drills.hint: 'Past' rhymes with 'fast'. Stress the content words: 'GO PAST the HOSpital and TURN LEFT.' Small words like 'the' and 'and' are quick and soft.

roleplay.context: You are practising giving directions with Mr. Khoirul. He is at the bus station and wants to go to the shopping mall. You must explain the route using movement prepositions: along, past, across, and into. Speak clearly and use falling intonation for each direction.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! Today we will practise giving directions using movement prepositions. Are you ready?
turns.translation: Halo! Hari ini kita akan berlatih memberikan petunjuk arah menggunakan preposisi pergerakan. Apakah kamu siap?

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Great! Imagine I am at the bus station. How do I get to the shopping mall? Use 'walk along' in your answer.
turns.translation: Bagus! Bayangkan saya di halte bus. Bagaimana cara saya ke pusat perbelanjaan? Gunakan 'walk along' dalam jawabanmu.

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Walk along Park Street for about five minutes.
turns.translation: Berjalanlah menyusuri Jalan Park selama sekitar lima menit.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Perfect! Now, what do I do after that? Use 'go past' this time.
turns.translation: Sempurna! Sekarang, apa yang harus saya lakukan setelah itu? Gunakan 'go past' kali ini.

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Go past the hospital and turn left.
turns.translation: Lewati rumah sakit dan belok kiri.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Excellent! One more direction. Tell me to cross something using 'across' and enter something using 'into'.
turns.translation: Luar biasa! Satu petunjuk arah lagi. Suruh saya menyeberangi sesuatu menggunakan 'across' dan masuk ke sesuatu menggunakan 'into'.

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: Walk across the parking lot and go into the main entrance. The mall is there!
turns.translation: Berjalanlah menyeberangi tempat parkir dan masuk ke pintu masuk utama. Pusat perbelanjaannya ada di sana!

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your walk from home to school. Use at least three movement prepositions: into, across, and along. Follow the story points below.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please tell me about your walk from home to school. Describe the route step by step. Use movement prepositions like into, across, and along.
storyPoints: First, describe leaving your house and walking along a street.
Then, describe crossing something, like a bridge or a road, using 'across'.
Finally, describe arriving and going into the school building.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I walk out of my house and walk along the main road. Then I walk across the bridge. Finally, I go into the school building.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wɔːk aʊt əv maɪ haʊs ənd wɔːk əˈlɒŋ ðə meɪn rəʊd. ðen aɪ wɔːk əˈkrɒs ðə brɪdʒ. ˈfaɪ.nə.li aɪ ɡəʊ ˈɪn.tə ðə skuːl ˈbɪl.dɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to stress the second syllable in 'across' and 'along'. Use falling intonation at the end of each sentence because you are describing actions.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task checks if you can use multiple movement prepositions in a connected narrative. Each story point guides you to use a different preposition in a logical order.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about going to the park last weekend. Use at least three movement prepositions: through, past, and into. Follow the story points below.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell me about a trip to the park. How did you get there? What did you walk through or past? Use movement prepositions in your story.
storyPoints: First, describe walking past a shop or building on the way to the park.
Then, describe going through a gate or a garden to enter the park.
Finally, describe going into a café or a playground inside the park.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I walked past the bookshop on Main Street. Then I went through the big gate. Finally, I went into the café in the park.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wɔːkt pɑːst ðə ˈbʊk.ʃɒp ɒn meɪn striːt. ðen aɪ went θruː ðə bɪɡ ɡeɪt. ˈfaɪ.nə.li aɪ went ˈɪn.tə ðə ˈkæf.eɪ ɪn ðə pɑːk/
practicumQuestions.hint: When you say 'through', put your tongue between your teeth for the /θ/ sound. Link 'went into' smoothly: 'went-IN-tuh'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises telling a route story using 'past', 'through', and 'into'. The story points help you organise your ideas in a clear sequence using movement prepositions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are a tourist at a train station. Mr. Khoirul is a local person. Ask him for directions to the museum. He will give you directions, and you must repeat them back using movement prepositions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! You look lost. Where do you want to go? I can help you find the way.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are standing at the train station in a small town. You want to visit the museum but you do not know the way. A friendly local person, Mr. Khoirul, offers to help. You need to ask for directions and then confirm the route by repeating it back using movement prepositions like along, across, and into.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly local person who knows the town very well. He speaks slowly and clearly. He gives simple directions using movement prepositions and asks you to repeat them.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Excuse me, how do I get to the museum? So I walk along this street, go across the square, and go into the museum?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪkˈskjuːz miː, haʊ duː aɪ ɡet tə ðə mjuːˈziː.əm? səʊ aɪ wɔːk əˈlɒŋ ðɪs striːt, ɡəʊ əˈkrɒs ðə skweər, ənd ɡəʊ ˈɪn.tə ðə mjuːˈziː.əm/
practicumQuestions.hint: When asking for directions, use rising intonation: 'How do I get to the museum?' ↗ When repeating directions back, use falling intonation because you are confirming.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises asking for and confirming directions in a real-life situation. You must use movement prepositions correctly while also practising question intonation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are helping Mr. Khoirul find his way from the library to the post office. Give him step-by-step directions using movement prepositions: out of, along, and past.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Excuse me, I am at the library right now. Can you tell me how to get to the post office? Please give me step-by-step directions.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Mr. Khoirul is inside the library and needs to go to the post office. You know the route well. You need to give him clear directions using 'out of' to leave the library, 'along' for the street, and 'past' for a landmark on the way.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a visitor who does not know the area. He is polite and will ask you to repeat or clarify if your directions are not clear. He may ask follow-up questions like 'Which side of the street?' or 'How far?'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Go out of the library and turn right. Walk along Green Street. Go past the supermarket. The post office is on your left.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɡəʊ aʊt əv ðə ˈlaɪ.brər.i ənd tɜːn raɪt. wɔːk əˈlɒŋ ɡriːn striːt. ɡəʊ pɑːst ðə ˈsuː.pə.mɑː.kɪt. ðə pəʊst ˈɒf.ɪs ɪz ɒn jɔːr left/
practicumQuestions.hint: Say 'out of' as one smooth unit: 'OWT-uv'. Use falling intonation for each direction sentence because you are giving commands.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay tests your ability to give clear, step-by-step directions using movement prepositions. Practise linking 'out of' and stressing content words.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You and Mr. Khoirul are planning a walking tour of the city. Describe a route that goes through a park, across a river, and into a famous building. Take turns suggesting parts of the route.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Let's plan a walking tour together! I will start. First, we walk along the main road. Now, what is the next part of the route? Use 'through' in your answer.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and Mr. Khoirul are sitting at a café and planning a walking tour of the city for tomorrow. You have a simple map in front of you. You take turns describing different parts of the route. You need to use movement prepositions: through, across, and into.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is your friend and tour planning partner. He suggests some parts of the route and asks you to suggest other parts. He is enthusiastic and encouraging. He will prompt you to use specific prepositions.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Then we walk through the park. After that, we go across the old bridge over the river. Finally, we go into the history museum.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðen wiː wɔːk θruː ðə pɑːk. ˈɑːf.tər ðæt, wiː ɡəʊ əˈkrɒs ðiː əʊld brɪdʒ ˈəʊ.vər ðə ˈrɪv.ər. ˈfaɪ.nə.li wiː ɡəʊ ˈɪn.tə ðə ˈhɪs.tər.i mjuːˈziː.əm/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use sequence words like 'then', 'after that', and 'finally' to connect your directions. This makes your route description clear and easy to follow.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This collaborative roleplay practises planning and describing a route using movement prepositions. Using sequence words with prepositions shows good speaking organisation at A1 level.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Mr. Khoirul is a delivery driver. He calls you to ask for directions to your house. Guide him from the main road to your front door using movement prepositions: along, past, through, and into.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! I have a package for you. I am on the main road now. Can you tell me how to get to your house from here? Please be very clear!
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A delivery driver, Mr. Khoirul, is calling you on the phone. He is on the main road near your neighbourhood but cannot find your house. You need to guide him step by step using movement prepositions. He might ask you to repeat or slow down.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul is a friendly but slightly confused delivery driver. He is driving slowly and needs very clear, simple directions. He will confirm each step before moving to the next one. He may say things like 'OK, and then?' or 'Can you repeat that?'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Drive along the main road. Go past the petrol station. Turn left and drive through the small gate. Come into the parking area. My house is the blue one.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /draɪv əˈlɒŋ ðə meɪn rəʊd. ɡəʊ pɑːst ðə ˈpet.rəl ˈsteɪ.ʃən. tɜːn left ənd draɪv θruː ðə smɔːl ɡeɪt. kʌm ˈɪn.tə ðə ˈpɑː.kɪŋ ˈeə.ri.ə. maɪ haʊs ɪz ðə bluː wʌn/
practicumQuestions.hint: Speak slowly and clearly, as if you are really on the phone. Pause between each direction to let the driver follow. Use falling intonation for each instruction.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This phone-call roleplay is very practical. Giving directions over the phone requires extra clarity. Practise pausing between steps and stressing the prepositions so the listener understands the movement.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on using the correct movement preposition. The sentence describes someone leaving a building.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the movement preposition.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: The cat jumped out of the window and ran across the garden.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðə kæt dʒʌmpt aʊt əv ðə ˈwɪn.dəʊ ənd ræn əˈkrɒs ðə ˈɡɑː.dən/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember: 'out of' means moving from inside to outside. 'Across' means moving from one side to the other side. Link 'out of' together as 'OWT-uv'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill tests your understanding and pronunciation of two key movement prepositions: 'out of' (leaving an enclosed space) and 'across' (moving from one side to the other). Using them together in one sentence shows you understand the difference.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on the correct word order: verb + preposition of movement + place. Make sure you do not add extra words between the preposition and the place.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence. Be careful with the grammar: verb plus preposition plus place.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: She walked through the forest and went into the village.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ʃiː wɔːkt θruː ðə ˈfɒr.ɪst ənd went ˈɪn.tə ðə ˈvɪl.ɪdʒ/
practicumQuestions.hint: The grammar pattern is: subject + verb + preposition + the + place. For example: 'She walked through the forest.' Do not say 'She walked to through the forest.' The preposition comes directly after the verb.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill focuses on the correct A1 grammar structure for movement prepositions. The pattern is always: verb of movement + preposition + noun phrase. Common errors include adding extra prepositions like 'to' before the movement preposition.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on the syllable stress of the underlined words. 'Across' is stressed on the second syllable: a-CROSS. 'Into' is stressed on the first syllable: IN-to.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the stress pattern. 'Across' has stress on the second syllable. 'Into' has stress on the first syllable. Now say the sentence.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: We walked across the playground and went into the classroom.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wiː wɔːkt əˈkrɒs ðə ˈpleɪ.ɡraʊnd ənd went ˈɪn.tə ðə ˈklɑːs.ruːm/
practicumQuestions.hint: Tap your hand on the stressed syllable: a-CROSS (tap on CROSS), IN-to (tap on IN). Also notice: PLAY-ground (tap on PLAY) and CLASS-room (tap on CLASS). Compound nouns are stressed on the first part.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises syllable stress patterns. 'Across' and 'along' are stressed on the second syllable, but 'into' and 'out of' are stressed on the first syllable. Getting the stress right helps listeners understand which preposition you are using.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following two sentences out loud. The first is a question (rising intonation ↗). The second is a direction command (falling intonation ↘). Show the difference clearly with your voice.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now practise intonation. The question goes UP at the end. The direction goes DOWN at the end. Say both sentences and make the difference clear.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Do I go across the bridge? Yes, walk across the bridge and go into the park.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /duː aɪ ɡəʊ əˈkrɒs ðə brɪdʒ ↗ jes, wɔːk əˈkrɒs ðə brɪdʒ ənd ɡəʊ ˈɪn.tə ðə pɑːk ↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: For the question 'Do I go across the bridge?', your voice should rise at the end on 'bridge?' ↗ For the answer 'Walk across the bridge and go into the park.', your voice should fall at the end on 'park.' ↘ This is the difference between asking and telling.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises the difference between rising intonation (yes/no questions) and falling intonation (commands and instructions). When giving directions, you use falling intonation because you are telling someone what to do. When confirming directions, you use rising intonation because you are asking if you understood correctly.
